lead: The risen Lord stands among his frightened disciples and says, “Peace be with you.” Paul, writing to the Colossians, prays that this peace of Christ may rule in their hearts, and that the word of Christ may dwell in them richly as they sing and give thanks. The Gospel shows that the peace is not an idea but a person: Jesus with real hands and feet, who eats before them. The words to watch are peace, thankful and flesh and bones.

r.h: Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor. The letter tells the believers that they have been raised with Christ and must now “seek the things that are above” (3:1). Paul then describes the new life as a change of clothes: take off the old self, put on the new (3:9–12). Today’s verses are the crowning garment and what follows from it.

Many scholars think that Colossians was written by a disciple of Paul in his name; others hold that Paul wrote it himself, perhaps with a co-worker. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
str: v. 14: above all, love, which binds everything together.
v. 15: the peace of Christ as the umpire of the heart; be thankful.
v. 16: the word of Christ dwelling richly; teaching and singing.
v. 17: do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks.
kw: Love is the belt that holds all the other virtues in place, so that together they make one whole. Without love the other virtues fall apart.
A word from the games: the umpire who decides. When the heart is divided, the peace of Christ is to give the decision.
Thanks is named three times in these four verses (vv. 15, 16, 17). The Greek word is the root of “Eucharist”, the great thanksgiving of the Church.
vv: Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
The Greek has no new verb here; “clothe yourselves” carries on from v. 12. Love is the last and outer garment that holds the rest together.
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in the one body. And be thankful.
This peace is not only inner calm. We are called to it “in the one body”, the Church; it is peace among brothers and sisters.
with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
Singing is one of the ways the word of Christ lives in a community. The early Church prayed the psalms and also composed new hymns to Christ.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father, a blessing by which the Church expresses her gratitude for all his benefits (CCC 1359–1360). Paul’s words also describe the Church’s prayer: the word, the psalms, the hymns and thanksgiving all meet in the Liturgy. In the Holy Qurbana the priest greets the people more than once with the risen Lord’s own words, “Peace be with you”, so that his peace may rule among us.

r.h: See that it is I myself
set: It is still Easter Sunday evening in Luke’s account. The two disciples have returned from Emmaus and are telling how they knew the Lord in the breaking of the bread (24:35). The eleven and those with them have just said, “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). And while they are talking, he is there.
str: v. 36: Jesus stands among them: “Peace be with you.”
vv. 37–38: fear: they think they see a ghost.
vv. 39–40: hands and feet: “Touch me and see.”
vv. 41–43: joy mixed with disbelief; Jesus eats a piece of fish.
kw: The everyday greeting shalom, now spoken by one who has passed through death. In the risen Lord’s mouth it is the gift of reconciliation.
The disciples think they are seeing a spirit without a body. Jesus corrects them: the Resurrection is not a vision or a ghost story.
Jesus insists on the reality of his body. It is the same body that was crucified, now glorified.
vv: While they were talking about this, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
A few ancient manuscripts lack the words “and said to them, ‘Peace be with you’”, but almost all have them, and they match John 20:19.
Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
The wounds show who he is. The risen Lord does not leave behind his Passion; he carries it into glory.
While in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering
An honest line. Joy can be so great that it is hard to believe. Faith grows slowly, and the Lord is patient with it.
and he took it and ate in their presence.
He does not need food; he eats for them, to show that he is truly alive. Peter later preaches that the apostles “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the risen Jesus showed the disciples that he was not a ghost, invited them to touch him, and ate with them, and that his body is the same body that suffered and died, now risen with new properties (CCC 645). Christ rose with his own body, and so shall we (CCC 999). St Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom, defends this against those who said the Lord only seemed to have a body: he was in the flesh even after the Resurrection, and the apostles touched him and believed (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 3, in substance).

qa: If his body was real, how could he suddenly stand among them, or come in through locked doors (John 20:19)?

The risen body of Jesus is real, but it is no longer bound by space and time in the way our bodies are. It is a glorified body, sharing in the life of the Spirit. It is not a return to earthly life, as with Lazarus (CCC 645–646). This is why the disciples sometimes did not recognize him at first, and why he could come and go as he willed.
study: Paul says that the peace of Christ should be the umpire in my heart. Which decision before me now needs that umpire?
Jesus showed his wounds to frightened friends. How can my own healed wounds help someone else to believe?
